issues.legal_issue: Income derived from land is agricultural income only when it results from cultivation involving basic operations on the land, together with any subsequent operations that form part of the same integrated activity.
material_facts: The forest was originally of spontaneous growth, and much of the work performed there consisted of tending, protecting and maintaining trees that had not been planted through basic agricultural operations.
The forest also had areas that became denuded and were replanted, after which the planted trees were tended and maintained.
issues.conclusion: Agriculture requires basic operations on the land that cause produce to be raised; subsequent operations can be agricultural when they continue those basic operations, but cannot by themselves make the income from spontaneously grown products agricultural income. The produce need not be food: useful products of the land, including timber and forest trees, can qualify when raised by agriculture.
issues.legal_principle: Under section 2(1) of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922, read with the exemption in section 4(3)(viii), income must be derived from land used for agricultural purposes and by agriculture or the specified related processes. Agriculture denotes an integrated activity whose essential foundation is basic operations on the land, such as tilling, sowing or planting; later operations such as weeding, tending, pruning and harvesting count when connected with those basic operations. Products of the land may include commercial and forest products, but activities merely connected with land, such as livestock rearing or dairy farming, do not thereby become agriculture. The Court applied the test stated by the Privy Council in Raja Mustafa Ali Khan v. Commissioner of Income-tax, U.P., Ajmer and Ajmer-Merwara, and distinguished income from products of spontaneous growth that involved no agricultural operations.

predicates.income_tax_exemption_claim: A taxpayer claims that income derived from land is exempt as agricultural income.
predicates.basic_land_operations: A cultivator tills, sows, plants or performs similar foundational operations on the land.
predicates.produce_raised_by_those_operations: The foundational operations cause useful produce to be raised from the land.

issues.definition: When a taxpayer claims an agricultural-income exemption and foundational operations on the land raise useful produce, the income is agricultural.

issues.legal_issue: Income from a partly spontaneous forest can be agricultural income to the extent it derives from trees planted and raised through agricultural operations, and failure to establish the non-agricultural share may prevent reversal of an exemption ruling.
material_facts: The forest was about 150 years old and originally of spontaneous growth, but portions became denuded and the owner planted fresh trees in those areas.
Staff performed forestry work including pruning, weeding, felling, clearing, cutting channels, guarding trees and sowing seeds after digging soil in denuded areas.
The expenditure shown for maintaining the forest was substantial in relation to its total income.

The tax authorities did not ascertain what portion of the income came from planted trees and what portion came from spontaneous growth; the Court considered a fresh inquiry undesirable after the long lapse of time.
issues.conclusion: Income derived from the trees planted by the owner was agricultural income. Because the Department had not established what portion of the income came from spontaneous growth, and the circumstances indicated that a substantial portion came from planted trees, the Court found no basis to reverse the decision below and dismissed the appeal.
issues.legal_principle: Under sections 2(1) and 4(3)(viii) of the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922, trees raised through basic agricultural operations can yield exempt agricultural income, whereas income from spontaneous growth is not agricultural merely because the trees are maintained or protected. Applying the cultivation test in Raja Mustafa Ali Khan v. Commissioner of Income-tax, U.P., Ajmer and Ajmer-Merwara, the Court held that the planted-tree income qualified; the Department's failure to establish the non-agricultural portion, together with the record and the undesirability of a fresh inquiry, meant the appeal could not succeed.

predicates.income_tax_appeal: A revenue authority appeals a ruling that forest income is exempt as agricultural income.
predicates.forest_originally_spontaneous: The forest initially grew without being raised through human agricultural operations.
predicates.trees_planted_in_denuded_areas: The owner planted trees in areas where the forest had become denuded.
predicates.substantial_forest_maintenance_expenditu: The owner incurred substantial expenditure on maintaining and regenerating the forest.
predicates.department_failed_to_separate_income_sou: The tax authority did not establish what income came from planted trees and what came from spontaneous growth.
predicates.fresh_inquiry_undesirable: The court considers a new inquiry unsuitable because of the lapse of time.

issues.definition: A revenue appeal fails where a partly spontaneous forest includes planted trees, substantial maintenance expenditure supports a substantial planted-tree contribution, the authority did not separate the income sources, and a fresh inquiry is unsuitable.

issues.legal_issue: The constitutional allocation of agriculture and forests to separate legislative subjects does not make those subjects mutually exclusive for determining whether forest income falls within the definition of agricultural income.
material_facts: The argument against exemption relied on the Constitution listing agriculture and forests as separate legislative subjects.
The applicable definition of agricultural income was the definition in the income-tax legislation, and the constitutional provisions also included a separate subject for taxes on agricultural income.
issues.conclusion: The separate legislative entries for agriculture and forests do not exclude forestry income from the agricultural-income category when that income meets the statutory definition.
issues.legal_principle: The Court construed Entries 14, 19 and 46 of List II of the Seventh Schedule to the Constitution as legislative heads that are not mutually exclusive. Article 366(1) refers to agricultural income as defined for the purposes of enactments relating to Indian income tax; accordingly, the statutory definition in section 2(1) of the Indian Income-tax Act determines whether qualifying forestry income is agricultural income within the relevant constitutional tax entry.

predicates.constitutional_entry_dispute: A party argues that separate constitutional subjects for agriculture and forests exclude forestry from agriculture.
predicates.forest_income_meets_agricultural_income_: Income from forestry satisfies the statutory definition of agricultural income.

issues.definition: When forest income satisfies the agricultural-income definition, separate legislative subjects for forests and agriculture do not exclude it from the agricultural-income tax category.
